screens.title: Event‑Driven Interaction Systems
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn how to make objects in your game respond to player intent without tight coupling. We focus on two complementary C++ patterns in Unreal Engine: UInterface-based contracts that describe what an object can do, and dynamic multicast delegates, often called event dispatchers, that let objects broadcast state changes to many listeners. You will see how an Interactable interface defines functions like Interact and CanInteract, how to implement these functions in a specific actor such as a door, and how your character can safely discover and call those interface functions after a trace. Then we cover how to declare and broadcast an event dispatcher, and how other actors or widgets can bind to that dispatcher using AddDynamic. Along the way we highlight common pitfalls — for example, the correct way to call BlueprintNativeEvent functions and lifecycle issues with bindings. By the end you will know when to use a direct call, an interface, or a delegate, and how these pieces fit together to build a flexible interaction system.

screens.title: What is a UInterface?
screens.narratorSegment: A UInterface in Unreal Engine is an engine-aware C++ interface that defines a contract of functions a UObject-derived class can implement. Practically, it splits into two pieces: the UObject-derived UINTERFACE wrapper and the C++ interface class, which declares functions marked with UFUNCTION. When you mark functions as BlueprintNativeEvent, you allow a default C++ implementation to exist via a function with the _Implementation suffix while still allowing Blueprint overrides. The primary benefit is polymorphism without inheritance: any AActor, whether ADoor, APickup, or ANPC, can declare it implements the Interactable interface and provide its own behavior. A concrete example is Interact(AActor* Interactor) and CanInteract(AActor* Interactor). Implementing classes provide Interact_Implementation and CanInteract_Implementation to offer behavior. A common misconception is treating Cast to the concrete class instead of casting to the interface; that reduces flexibility. Another pitfall is calling the interface function directly rather than using Execute_ when the callee might be a Blueprint implementation. Key takeaway: UInterface gives you a stable A P I that multiple different classes can implement, enabling you to write interaction code that operates on contracts instead of concrete types.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a UInterface?
UInterface explained
  • Defines a contract of functions any UObject can implement.
  • Split into UINTERFACE wrapper and C++ interface class.
  • Use BlueprintNativeEvent to allow C++ defaults and Blueprint overrides.
Key Takeaway

Prefer interfaces when you want multiple unrelated classes to expose the same API without shared inheritance.

Common mistake
Casting to a concrete class instead of the interface reduces reusability. Use Cast<IInteractableInterface> or Implements<UInteractableInterface> checks.
Concrete example: Interface functions
// InteractableInterface.h
UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable) class UInteractableInterface : public UInterface { GENERATED_BODY() };
class IInteractableInterface { GENERATED_BODY()
public:
	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	void Interact(AActor* Interactor);
	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	bool CanInteract(AActor* Interactor) const;
};
This header declares the contract. Implementers provide Interact_Implementation and CanInteract_Implementation in C++ or override in Blueprint.

screens.title: Creating InteractableInterface.h
screens.narratorSegment: When you create an Interactable interface, the header declares the UINTERFACE wrapper and the IInterface class with UFUNCTIONs for Interact and CanInteract. The BlueprintNativeEvent specifier is crucial: it tells the engine you may provide a C++ default implementation while still permitting Blueprint overrides. In practice this yields two ways to call the function safely. If you have a raw UObject pointer that implements the interface, the safe route is to use Execute_Interact on that object, which ensures the call reaches the Blueprint override or the C++ _Implementation as appropriate. A common misconception is to call a native C++ method directly on the interface pointer; that bypasses Blueprint routing. The concrete header shown in the chapter sets up Interact and CanInteract. After creating this header, implementers add Interact_Implementation in their. cpp files. Note the comment in the source that the UINTERFACE class itself requires little change; the action happens in the IInterface declaration and the implementing classes. Try creating the two files and confirm they compile before wiring the character input. Creating InteractableInterface.h means it enables both a c++ default implementation and blueprint overrides, and execute_ calls route correctly to either implementation.. In practical terms, syntax and why blueprintnativeevent matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Creating InteractableInterface.h
Header example
#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "UObject/Interface.h"
#include "InteractableInterface.generated.h"

UINTERFACE(MinimalAPI, Blueprintable)
class UInteractableInterface : public UInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()
};

class IInteractableInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()

public:
	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	void Interact(AActor* Interactor);

	UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent, BlueprintCallable, Category = "Interaction")
	bool CanInteract(AActor* Interactor) const;
};
Notes
  • Blueprintable allows Blueprints to implement the interface.
  • Provide C++ defaults by implementing Interact_Implementation in a .cpp file.
  • Call implementations via Execute_ helpers to support Blueprint overrides.
Concrete example & quick checklist
Checklist to finish before moving on:
  1. Create InteractableInterface.h and .cpp files.
  2. Mark functions BlueprintNativeEvent and BlueprintCallable.
  3. Compile and inspect generated Execute_ helpers in Intellisense.

When you expose CanInteract, you can easily hide or disable prompts based on runtime state without changing actor class types.

screens.title: Implementing Interact in ADoor
screens.narratorSegment: Once the interface exists, an actor like ADoor implements the contract by inheriting the IInteractableInterface and defining Interact_Implementation and CanInteract_Implementation. The ADoor header adds the interface to the class inheritance line. In the ADoor. cpp file you implement Interact_Implementation to toggle door state, play an animation, and optionally call OnDoorOpened. Broadcast if you expose a dispatcher. A concrete ADoor Interact_Implementation often logs a message so you can confirm the interaction during testing. It is important to implement CanInteract_Implementation to return whether the object is currently interactable, for example not locked or already open. A frequent misconception is trying to call Interact() directly on the interface pointer; instead, when you have a UObject pointer, use Execute_Interact to route correctly to C++ or Blueprint. Finally, if you want other systems to react when the door opens, expose an event dispatcher and Broadcast after changing state. Implementing Interact in ADoor means implement the interface on adoor with interact_implementation and caninteract_implementation; use broadcast when you want to notify listeners.. In practical terms, how an actor provides behavior for the interface. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Implementing Interact in ADoor
ADoor header / inheritance
// ADoor.h
#include "InteractableInterface.h"

UCLASS()
class ADoor : public AActor, public IInteractableInterface
{
	GENERATED_BODY()
public:
	virtual void Interact_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) override;
	virtual bool CanInteract_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) const override;
};
ADoor.cpp / example behaviour
// ADoor.cpp
void ADoor::Interact_Implementation(AActor* Interactor)
{
	// Toggle open/close state and play animation
	bIsOpen = !bIsOpen;
	UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Door interacted by %s!"), *Interactor->GetName());
	// Optionally: OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this);
}

bool ADoor::CanInteract_Implementation(AActor* Interactor) const
{
	return !bIsLocked;
}
Test the log to confirm the function runs. Use CanInteract to gate interactions and hide prompts when false.

screens.title: Character Trace → Interface Discovery
screens.narratorSegment: Your character's trace logic is the glue that discovers interactable actors. After performing a line or sphere trace, check whether the hit actor implements UInteractableInterface using Implements () or Cast (). If it does, store a TScriptInterface as CurrentInteractableActor. TScriptInterface holds both the UObject pointer and the interface pointer and plays nicely with garbage collection. When no hit is detected, clear the TScriptInterface to avoid stale references. A common error is keeping raw pointers to actors without UPROPERTY, which can lead to garbage collection surprises or dangling references. Another mistake is assuming a successful trace means the object is currently interactable; always call Execute_CanInteract with the stored object to check runtime state before calling Execute_Interact. This process yields a robust flow: trace, verify interface, set TScriptInterface, check CanInteract at input, and execute the interaction. Character Trace → Interface Discovery means trace for actors, verify implements<uinteractableinterface>(), and store as tscriptinterface to call execute_ helpers safely.. In practical terms, find an implementer and store it safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Character Trace → Interface Discovery
Step sequence
1. Perform trace (line or sphere) and get HitResult.
2. If HitActor && HitActor->Implements<UInteractableInterface>() then proceed.
3. Set CurrentInteractableActor.SetObject(HitActor); SetInterface(Cast<IInteractableInterface>(HitActor));
4. When input occurs, call Execute_CanInteract with CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject() before Execute_Interact.
Example snippet
if (NewHitActor && NewHitActor->Implements())
{
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetObject(NewHitActor);
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetInterface(Cast(NewHitActor));
}
else
{
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetObject(nullptr);
	CurrentInteractableActor.SetInterface(nullptr);
}
Clearing the interface when no hit prevents accidental Execute_ calls on invalid objects.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Binding Player Input & InteractInput
SetupPlayerInputComponent
void AMyCharacter::SetupPlayerInputComponent(UInputComponent* PlayerInputComponent)
{
	Super::SetupPlayerInputComponent(PlayerInputComponent);
	PlayerInputComponent->BindAction("Interact", IE_Pressed, this, &AMyCharacter::InteractInput);
}
InteractInput implementation
void AMyCharacter::InteractInput()
{
	if (CurrentInteractableActor)
	{
		if (CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_CanInteract(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this))
		{
			CurrentInteractableActor->Execute_Interact(CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject(), this);
		}
		else
		{
			UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Cannot interact with %s right now."), *CurrentInteractableActor.GetObject()->GetName());
		}
	}
}
Using GetObject ensures the Execute_ calls can route to Blueprint or C++ implementations correctly.

screens.title: Event Dispatchers (Delegates)
screens.narratorSegment: Event dispatchers, declared via macros like DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam, provide a one-to-many notification system. You declare a signature type and expose a UPROPERTY marked BlueprintAssignable so Blueprints can bind to it. In C++ listeners bind using AddDynamic with a method pointer. When the broadcaster calls Broadcast, every bound listener receives the notification. This pattern is ideal when the broadcaster should not know or care who is listening, such as a door actor notifying a sound emitter or a UI widget when it opens. Two practical cautions apply. First, if no listeners are bound, Broadcast silently does nothing — ensure important state changes are handled locally as well. Second, manage bindings across object lifecycle; remove bindings or rely on UObject lifecycle to avoid attempting to call into destroyed listeners. Broadcast is the method to trigger all listeners at once, and AddDynamic is the safe C++ binding method to use with dynamic multicast delegates. Event Dispatchers (Delegates) means use declare_dynamic_multicast_delegate to let actors broadcast events, and bind listeners with adddynamic or blueprint assignment.. In practical terms, declare, broadcast, and bind for one‑to‑many communication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

You declare a signature type and expose a UPROPERTY marked BlueprintAssignable so Blueprints can bind to it. In C++ listeners bind using AddDynamic with a method pointer. When the broadcaster calls Broadcast, every bound listener receives the notification. This pattern is ideal when the broadcaster should not know or care who is listening, such as a door actor notifying a sound emitter or a UI widget when it opens. Two practical cautions apply. First, if no listeners are bound, Broadcast silently does nothing — ensure important state changes are handled locally as well. Second, manage bindings across object lifecycle; remove bindings or rely on UObject lifecycle to avoid attempting to call into destroyed listeners. Broadcast is the method to trigger all listeners at once, and AddDynamic is the safe C++ binding method to use with dynamic multicast delegates. Event Dispatchers (Delegates) means use declare_dynamic_multicast_delegate to let actors broadcast events, and bind listeners with adddynamic or blueprint assignment.. In practical terms, declare, broadcast, and bind for one‑to‑many communication. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Declaration example
// In ADoor.h
DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FDoorOpenedSignature, AActor*, DoorActor);

UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable, Category = "Interaction")
FDoorOpenedSignature OnDoorOpened;
Marking as BlueprintAssignable makes it easy to connect listeners in Blueprint, while AddDynamic handles C++ bindings.
Broadcasting & binding
// Broadcast inside Interact_Implementation
OnDoorOpened.Broadcast(this);

// Bind in C++
OnDoor->OnDoorOpened.AddDynamic(this, &ASoundEmitter::PlayDoorSound);
If listeners are not bound, Broadcast does nothing. Manage AddDynamic and RemoveDynamic to avoid invalid calls when listeners are destroyed.

screens.title: Direct Calls vs Interfaces vs Dispatchers
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between direct function calls, interface calls, and event dispatchers depends on coupling and the number of receivers. Direct calls are simplest when two objects have a strong, explicit relationship — for example, a weapon component calling a method on its owner. This is efficient but brittle if owners change. Interfaces are ideal when you need polymorphic behavior across unrelated types. Define an IInteractableInterface so your character can interact with doors, chests, and pickups through the same A P I without knowing their concrete types. Event dispatchers provide loose coupling for one‑to‑many scenarios. A health component can broadcast OnHealthChanged and any number of widgets or effects can listen. A common misconception is that delegates always replace interfaces; they do not. Delegates are about broadcasting events, not defining reusable action contracts. For each system, weigh whether the broadcaster must know its listeners. If yes and only one listener exists, direct calls may be fine. If many listeners or unknown listeners are possible, prefer a dispatcher. If polymorphic single‑target behavior is required, choose an interface. Direct Calls vs Interfaces vs Dispatchers means use direct calls for tight ownership, interfaces for polymorphic single targets, and dispatchers for one‑to‑many broadcasts.. In practical terms, choose the right communication pattern for coupling needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Direct Calls
Strong dependency, simple, use for owner/child relationships where the caller knows the callee type.
Example: WeaponComponent calling Owner->Reload()
Interfaces
Polymorphic contract for single-target interactions across many classes without inheritance coupling.
Example: Character calls Execute_Interact on any implementer.
Dispatchers
One-to-many notifications where the broadcaster should be ignorant of listeners.

Ask: How many listeners? Does the broadcaster need to know the listener? If many or unknown, use a dispatcher. If single and polymorphic, use an interface. If tightly coupled owner-child, use a direct call.

screens.narratorSegment: For more complex projects, consider an Interaction Manager or a component that centralizes trace, focus, and selection logic. Rather than scattering trace code across characters, a manager can own the sphere or line trace, track the currently highlighted interactable, and provide a single A P I for querying the best interactable under the crosshair. screens.title: Managing Delegate Bindings & Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Binding to dynamic multicast delegates is straightforward, but lifecycle management is critical. When you bind in C++ with AddDynamic, the binding stores a reference to the listener object. If the listener is destroyed and the binding is not removed, Broadcast later may attempt to call a function on a destroyed object. Unreal's garbage collection often clears UObject-based bindings, but you should still remove bindings proactively when listeners are about to be destroyed or when they no longer need updates. Use RemoveDynamic during EndPlay or in the listener's destructor-equivalent to be explicit. Another important practice is to check for bound listeners if your logic depends on at least one listener responding; Broadcast is safe when no listeners exist, but you might still want fallback behavior. A common pitfall is forgetting to use BlueprintAssignable for bindings in Blueprint, or forgetting that AddDynamic requires matching function signatures. The takeaway is to treat binding management as part of A P I design and to test binds and unbinds across actor lifecycle events. Managing Delegate Bindings & Lifecycle means always remove dynamic bindings when listeners are destroyed or no longer need updates; be explicit to avoid runtime errors.. In practical terms, avoid dangling bindings and crashes by removing dynamic bindings appropriately. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Binding & unbinding
Bind in BeginPlay or when the listener becomes relevant with AddDynamic, and unbind in EndPlay or when no longer needed with RemoveDynamic.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn how to make objects in your game respond to player intent without tight coupling. We focus on two complementary C++ patterns in Unreal Engine: UInterface-based contracts that describe what an object can do, and dynamic multicast delegates, often called event dispatchers, that let objects broadcast state changes to many listeners. You will see how an Interactable interface defines functions like Interact and CanInteract, how to implement these functions in a specific actor such as a door, and how your character can safely discover and call those interface functions after a trace. Then we cover how to declare and broadcast an event dispatcher, and how other actors or widgets can bind to that dispatcher using AddDynamic. Along the way we highlight common pitfalls — for example, the correct way to call BlueprintNativeEvent functions and lifecycle issues with bindings. By the end you will know when to use a direct call, an interface, or a delegate, and how these pieces fit together to build a flexible interaction system.

By the end of this chapter you will design and implement C++ interfaces that define interaction contracts, use event dispatchers for decoupled communication, and build character tracing that finds and triggers interaction logic. First, you will create a UInterface with BlueprintNativeEvent functions. This matters because it lets different actor classes present the same interaction A P I to your character without the character needing to know actor types. Second, you will declare and broadcast dynamic multicast delegates so one actor can notify many listeners. You will practice binding listeners and consider lifecycle issues to avoid dangling bindings. Third, you will implement an interaction flow that stores a TScriptInterface reference when a trace hits an interactable actor and then calls Execute_Interact from player input. Finally, you will compare direct function calls, interface calls, and event dispatchers so you can choose the right coupling level for different systems. Each objective includes a short checklist and a milestone to mark verified competency.

Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can validate your understanding. For the UInterface objective, implement InteractableInterface. h and provide Interact_Implementation on an ADoor actor. Test that the door logs a message when triggered. For event dispatchers, declare a delegate type, expose it as a BlueprintAssignable UPROPERTY, and broadcast from the actor; then bind a separate actor or widget to react. For trace storage, modify your character to hold a TScriptInterface named CurrentInteractableActor, set it when the trace hits, and clear it when the trace no longer hits. Finally, to choose the right coupling, complete a short design exercise: take three systems — a weapon owner call, a pickup interaction, and a health change UI — and justify whether you would use a direct call, an interface, or a delegate. These milestones map to the hands-on activity where you create the interface, implement ADoor, and wire the character input to Execute_Interact.

A UInterface in Unreal Engine is an engine-aware C++ interface that defines a contract of functions a UObject-derived class can implement. Practically, it splits into two pieces: the UObject-derived UINTERFACE wrapper and the C++ interface class, which declares functions marked with UFUNCTION. When you mark functions as BlueprintNativeEvent, you allow a default C++ implementation to exist via a function with the _Implementation suffix while still allowing Blueprint overrides. The primary benefit is polymorphism without inheritance: any AActor, whether ADoor, APickup, or ANPC, can declare it implements the Interactable interface and provide its own behavior. A concrete example is Interact(AActor* Interactor) and CanInteract(AActor* Interactor). Implementing classes provide Interact_Implementation and CanInteract_Implementation to offer behavior. A common misconception is treating Cast to the concrete class instead of casting to the interface; that reduces flexibility. Another pitfall is calling the interface function directly rather than using Execute_ when the callee might be a Blueprint implementation. Key takeaway: UInterface gives you a stable A P I that multiple different classes can implement, enabling you to write interaction code that operates on contracts instead of concrete types.

When you create an Interactable interface, the header declares the UINTERFACE wrapper and the IInterface class with UFUNCTIONs for Interact and CanInteract. The BlueprintNativeEvent specifier is crucial: it tells the engine you may provide a C++ default implementation while still permitting Blueprint overrides. In practice this yields two ways to call the function safely. If you have a raw UObject pointer that implements the interface, the safe route is to use Execute_Interact on that object, which ensures the call reaches the Blueprint override or the C++ _Implementation as appropriate. Event dispatchers, declared via macros like DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam, provide a one-to-many notification system. Choosing between direct function calls, interface calls, and event dispatchers depends on coupling and the number of receivers. Direct calls are simplest when two objects have a strong, explicit relationship — for example, a weapon component calling a method on its owner. This is efficient but brittle if owners change. Interfaces are ideal when you need polymorphic behavior across unrelated types. Define an IInteractableInterface so your character can interact with doors, chests, and pickups through the same A P I without knowing their concrete types. Event dispatchers provide loose coupling for one‑to‑many scenarios. A health component can broadcast OnHealthChanged and any number of widgets or effects can listen. A common misconception is that delegates always replace interfaces; they do not. Delegates are about broadcasting events, not defining reusable action contracts. For each system, weigh whether the broadcaster must know its listeners. If yes and only one listener exists, direct calls may be fine. If many listeners or unknown listeners are possible, prefer a dispatcher. If polymorphic single‑target behavior is required, choose an interface. Binding to dynamic multicast delegates is straightforward, but lifecycle management is critical. When you bind in C++ with AddDynamic, the binding stores a reference to the listener object. If the listener is destroyed and the binding is not removed, Broadcast later may attempt to call a function on a destroyed object. Unreal's garbage collection often clears UObject-based bindings, but you should still remove bindings proactively when listeners are about to be destroyed or when they no longer need updates. Use RemoveDynamic during EndPlay or in the listener's destructor-equivalent to be explicit. Another important practice is to check for bound listeners if your logic depends on at least one listener responding; Broadcast is safe when no listeners exist, but you might still want fallback behavior.
